labs.title: Explore Azure Cosmos DB Data Explorer for a NoSQL container
labs.summary: Create an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account, choose a partition key for an orders container, add a JSON order document, and query it in Data Explorer.
labs.scenario: Alpine Goods is building a product-catalog and orders feature where each order arrives as a JSON document and the application usually looks up orders by customer. In the **simulated Azure portal** on your lab VM, create an Azure Cosmos DB account using the **Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL** API, then use **Data Explorer** to create database **RetailDB** and container **Orders** with partition key **/customerId**. Add one shipped order document and query shipped orders. Everything is simulated - no real Azure subscription is used.
learningObjectives: Choose Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL for JSON document data instead of relational SQL
Create a database and container in Data Explorer with a partition key that fits access patterns
Add a document item and query it with Cosmos DB SQL syntax
Explain documents, key-value data, column-family data, graph data and when Cosmos DB differs from Azure SQL
prerequisites: Know that JSON documents can store nested properties and arrays

components.title: Choose the data model first
components.text: Azure Cosmos DB offers multiple APIs. For this lab, the application stores orders as JSON documents and queries them with the NoSQL query language.

items.label: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
items.description: Native document API for JSON data, SQL-style queries and partitioned containers.

items.label: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB
items.description: Use when the application is built for MongoDB wire protocol compatibility.

action.text: MongoDB API is plausible for document apps, but this lab asks for Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL and Data Explorer SQL queries.
Cassandra is a column-family API. This order scenario needs JSON documents and NoSQL queries.

items.label: Apache Gremlin
items.description: Graph workloads with vertices and edges.

action.text: Gremlin is for graph traversal. Orders and product catalog documents do not require graph edges in this scenario.
Table API is key-value oriented. This lab needs nested JSON documents and SQL-style document queries.
PostgreSQL is relational. Use Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL when the primary model is JSON documents with flexible schema.

components.text: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL stores JSON items in containers. A partition key distributes items into logical partitions so the service can scale horizontally.

components.title: Non-relational choices
components.text: Document databases store JSON documents. Key-value stores retrieve values by key. Column-family stores group sparse columns by row keys. Graph databases model vertices and edges. Cosmos DB for NoSQL is a good fit here because each order can be a self-contained JSON document with nested line items.

components.title: Cosmos DB query language
components.text: The NoSQL API stores documents and lets you query them with SQL keywords. In this lab engine, string literals use single quotes, nested paths such as `c.items` are supported, and document comparisons are case-sensitive.

sampleQueries.label: Shipped orders
sampleQueries.sql: SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.status = 'Shipped' ORDER BY c.id

sampleQueries.label: Projected customer orders
sampleQueries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.customerId, c.orderTotal FROM c WHERE c.customerId = 'cust-northwind-01' ORDER BY c.id

sampleQueries.label: Count shipped orders
sampleQueries.sql: SELECT COUNT(1) AS shippedOrders FROM c WHERE c.status = 'Shipped'

steps.title: Choose Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
steps.instruction: In the portal menu, select **Azure Cosmos DB**, select **+ Create**, then choose **Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL** from the API tiles.
steps.hint: The NoSQL API is the native JSON document API. MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table and PostgreSQL target different models or compatibility needs.
steps.explanation: Cosmos DB supports multiple data models. Documents are a strong fit when each order can be stored as a JSON item with nested line items. Azure SQL is better when the workload depends on normalized tables and relational constraints.

rules.description: You opened the Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL create wizard
rules.failureFeedback: Choose the Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL tile.

steps.title: Create the NoSQL account
steps.instruction: On **Basics**, create resource group **rg-cosmos-retail**, set **Account name** to **cosmos-retail-orders-01**, keep **API** as **Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL**, choose **(Europe) West Europe**, select **Provisioned throughput**, leave promotional and account throughput limit toggles off, keep global distribution off, and select **Review + create** then **Create**.
steps.hint: Provisioned throughput reserves request capacity measured in request units. Serverless is another option for intermittent request patterns, but use provisioned throughput for this lab.
steps.explanation: Request units, or RU/s, represent the work for reads, writes and queries. This simulation uses fictional training settings and avoids real prices or quota values.

rules.description: The Cosmos DB for NoSQL account exists
rules.failureFeedback: Create cosmos-retail-orders-01 as an Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account in rg-cosmos-retail.

steps.title: Open Data Explorer
steps.instruction: When deployment completes, select **Go to resource**, then select **Data Explorer**.
steps.hint: Data Explorer is in the account resource menu and is also available from the command bar in this simulation.
steps.explanation: Data Explorer lets you create databases and containers, add items and run queries without leaving the Azure portal.

rules.failureFeedback: Open the Cosmos DB account and select Data Explorer.

steps.title: Create RetailDB and the Orders container
steps.instruction: Select **New Container**. Choose **Create new**, set **Database id** to **RetailDB**, **Container id** to **Orders**, **Partition key** to **/customerId**, **Throughput mode** to **Autoscale**, and **Training throughput setting** to **Autoscale training profile**. Select **OK**.
steps.hint: Do not use /status or /country because low-cardinality partition keys can create hot partitions. /id is high-cardinality but not the best fit for customer order lookups.
steps.explanation: A partition key determines the logical partition for each item. /customerId has many possible values and groups a customer's orders, which matches the application's common access pattern.

rules.failureFeedback: Create RetailDB and Orders with partition key /customerId and Autoscale throughput mode.

rules.description: The Orders container has seeded JSON documents
rules.failureFeedback: The Orders document set was not initialized.

steps.title: Add a JSON order document
steps.instruction: In the **Orders | Items** view, select **New Item** and save an order with `id` **ord-2001**, `customerId` **cust-northwind-01**, `customerName` **Northwind Traders**, `status` **Shipped**, `country` **NL**, `orderTotal` **152**, `items[0].sku` **PACK-COMMUTER**, and `items[0].quantity` **2**.
steps.hint: The partition key property, customerId, must be present on the item because the container is partitioned by /customerId.
steps.explanation: A document can contain nested values and arrays. Unlike normalized relational tables, the order can keep line-item details inside the order document when that shape fits the application.

rules.description: The new shipped order document exists
rules.failureFeedback: Add ord-2001 with customerId cust-northwind-01 and status Shipped.

steps.title: Query shipped documents
steps.instruction: Select **New SQL Query** and run `SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.status = 'Shipped' ORDER BY c.id`.
steps.hint: Cosmos DB document queries use an alias such as c for the container. In this engine, string comparisons are case-sensitive.
steps.explanation: This query returns whole JSON documents whose status is Shipped. It is not joining normalized tables; each document carries its own order details.

rules.description: A shipped-orders document query was run

rule.pattern: SELECT \* FROM c WHERE c\.status = 'Shipped' ORDER BY c\.id

rules.failureFeedback: Run the shipped-orders query exactly as written.

steps.title: Run projection and aggregate queries
steps.instruction: Run `SELECT c.id, c.customerId, c.orderTotal FROM c WHERE c.customerId = 'cust-northwind-01' ORDER BY c.id`, then run `SELECT COUNT(1) AS shippedOrders FROM c WHERE c.status = 'Shipped'`.
steps.hint: Projection returns selected properties. COUNT summarizes matching documents.
steps.explanation: Cosmos DB queries can project document paths and aggregate documents. Azure SQL would normally model customers, orders and order lines as related tables; Cosmos DB favors documents and partition-aware access patterns.

labs.solution:
1. Select **Azure Cosmos DB**, select **+ Create**, then choose **Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL**.
2. **Basics**: Resource group **Create new** -> `rg-cosmos-retail`; Account name `cosmos-retail-orders-01`; API **Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL**; Location **(Europe) West Europe**; Capacity mode **Provisioned throughput**; leave promotional and throughput limit toggles off. Keep global distribution off, then **Review + create** -> **Create**.
3. Select **Go to resource**, then **Data Explorer**.
4. Select **New Container**. Choose **Create new**; Database id `RetailDB`; Container id `Orders`; Partition key `/customerId`; Throughput mode **Autoscale**; Training throughput setting **Autoscale training profile**; select **OK**.
5. In **Orders | Items**, select **New Item** and save `ord-2001`, `cust-northwind-01`, `Northwind Traders`, `Shipped`, `NL`, `152`, `PACK-COMMUTER`, and quantity `2`.
6. Select **New SQL Query** and run `SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.status = 'Shipped' ORDER BY c.id`.
7. Run `SELECT c.id, c.customerId, c.orderTotal FROM c WHERE c.customerId = 'cust-northwind-01' ORDER BY c.id`, then run `SELECT COUNT(1) AS shippedOrders FROM c WHERE c.status = 'Shipped'`.
